Moistened
mois´nd
v. (made moist; watered, as bones with marrow)
From moisten, to make damp. The word occurs once, in Job's description of the man who dies in full strength — a body still well supplied, brought to the grave in the middle of its prosperity.

Biblical Definition

Job is refuting the comfortable doctrine of his friends, that the wicked visibly suffer and the righteous visibly prosper, and he does it by describing two deaths. The first: “One dieth in his full strength, being wholly at ease and quiet” (Job 21:23), and then the detail that makes it vivid, “His breasts are full of milk, and his bones are moistened with marrow” (Job 21:24). This man was never reduced. He was well-fed to the end and died in his sleep. Against him Job sets the other: “And another dieth in the bitterness of his soul, and never eateth with pleasure” (Job 21:25). And then the levelling sentence: “They shall lie down alike in the dust, and the worms shall cover them” (Job 21:26). Job's argument is not that God is unjust; it is that his friends' scheme of visible retribution cannot be read off the surface of a life, because the grave takes the fat man and the bitter man together and tells the observer nothing. Marrow in Scripture is the sign of abundance — a feast of fat things full of marrow — and here it belongs to a man whose ease proves precisely nothing about his standing before God.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines moisten as to make damp; to wet in a small degree; and marrow as a soft oleaginous substance contained in the cavities of animal bones.

expand to see more

MOISTEN, v.t. To make damp; to wet in a small degree.

MARROW, n. A soft, oleaginous substance contained in the cavities of animal bones; the best or choicest part.

PROSPERITY, n. Advance or gain in anything good or desirable; successful progress in any business or enterprise.

RETRIBUTION, n. Repayment; return accommodated to the action; reward or punishment.

GRAVE, n. A pit or excavation in the earth, for the reception of a dead body; a tomb.

Key Scripture

Job 21:24 — "His breasts are full of milk, and his bones are moistened with marrow."

Job 21:23 — "One dieth in his full strength, being wholly at ease and quiet."

Job 21:25 — "And another dieth in the bitterness of his soul, and never eateth with pleasure."

Job 21:26 — "They shall lie down alike in the dust, and the worms shall cover them."

Modern Corruption

The prosperity of the wicked is explained away by promising visible reversal in this life, which is precisely the doctrine Job is dismantling and the doctrine his friends were rebuked for holding.

expand to see more

The error Job attacks in chapter 21 is not extinct; it is a growth industry. The teaching that faithfulness produces health and wealth, and that hardship signals hidden sin or insufficient faith, is the position of Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar restated in modern idiom — and the LORD tells them at the end of the book that they have not spoken of Him the thing that is right. Job's observation stands: some wicked men live at ease, die quietly with their bones full of marrow, and are buried with honour. Any doctrine that must deny this is denying what Scripture plainly records.

The opposite error is to conclude from the same facts that God does not judge. Job does not go there and neither does the canon. Psalm 73 walks the identical road — envy at the prosperity of the wicked, the confession that it was too painful until the Psalmist went into the sanctuary of God, and then the end: surely thou didst set them in slippery places. The Reformed answer holds both halves. Providence is not a mechanism readable from outward circumstances, and the final assize is certain. A man whose bones are moistened with marrow may be the most pitiable man alive, and nothing visible will tell you so.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shaqah (H8248), to water or moisten; moach (H4221), marrow; shalanan (H7946), at ease, quiet; aphar (H6083), dust.

expand to see more

Hebrew shaqah (H8248) — to give drink, water, moisten; Job 21:24.

Hebrew moach (H4221) — marrow; only here in the Hebrew Bible.

Hebrew shalanan (H7946) — wholly at ease, tranquil; the manner of that death.

Hebrew mar (H4751) — bitter; the soul of the second man.

Hebrew aphar (H6083) — dust; they shall lie down alike in it.

Usage

"“His bones are moistened with marrow” — the well-fed man at his death."

"“Another dieth in the bitterness of his soul” — the other end of the same argument."

"“They shall lie down alike in the dust” — what the grave reports."
